The word catwalk has two distinct meanings as a noun. Both refer to a narrow, elevated walkway — but in very different settings.

This is the most widely known meaning today. A catwalk is the long, narrow, raised platform that fashion models walk along during a fashion show, so that the audience seated on both sides can see the clothes up close.

Picture a rectangular room full of people sitting in rows. A long, elevated strip — like a raised path — cuts through the middle of the room. Models walk from one end to the other, turn around, and walk back. That strip is the catwalk.

Why is it called a "catwalk"? The name comes from the way cats walk — gracefully, placing one foot carefully in front of the other along a narrow surface. Models walk the same way on the runway: heel-to-toe, in a straight line, with a measured, elegant stride. So the word captures both the narrowness of the path and the style of walking.

Key things to know about a fashion catwalk:

  • It is raised above the floor so everyone in the audience has a clear view.
  • It is narrow — typically just wide enough for one person.
  • It is the centrepiece of a fashion show, also called a runway show.
  • The word runway is used interchangeably with catwalk in fashion. Both refer to the same thing.

Examples in sentences:

  • The designer's new collection was unveiled on the catwalk in Milan.
  • She walked the catwalk for the first time at Paris Fashion Week.
  • The models glided down the catwalk as photographers clicked away.

You might also hear people use catwalk to refer to the fashion world or high-end fashion culture in general — as a concept, not just a physical platform. For example: "That look belongs on the catwalk" means the outfit is so stylish and dramatic it would fit right into a high-fashion show.
Meaning 2: A Narrow Elevated Walkway (Industrial / Structural Use)

This is the older and more literal meaning of the word, and it is still actively used — just in a different world.

A catwalk here is a narrow, raised walkway built for workers to walk along in places where a full floor would be impractical or impossible. These are found:

  • In factories and warehouses — high above the main floor, giving workers access to machinery, pipes, or storage areas at height.
  • In theatres and concert halls — above the stage, allowing technicians to reach and adjust stage lights, speakers, and rigging without being seen by the audience.
  • On ships and oil rigs — narrow walkways running along the sides or upper structures of a vessel.
  • On bridges — underneath or along the side of a bridge, used by engineers for inspection and maintenance.
  • In sports stadiums — above the seating areas, used by camera operators and lighting crews.

These catwalks are typically made of metal grating, have railings on both sides, and are built purely for practical access — not for comfort. They are not wide enough for two people to pass each other easily. They exist because the work needs to happen at height, and a full floor would be too expensive, too heavy, or simply unnecessary.

Examples in sentences:

  • The electrician climbed up to the catwalk above the stage to fix the spotlight.
  • Workers wearing safety harnesses crossed the catwalk over the factory floor.
  • The theatre's catwalk gave the crew access to the lighting grid.
The Connection Between the Two Meanings

Both meanings share the same core idea: a narrow, raised walkway that you walk carefully along. The fashion catwalk borrowed its name from the industrial one — which itself got its name from the way a cat walks along a narrow ledge. So the word has a clear visual logic: something narrow and elevated that requires careful, deliberate movement.

Fashion CatwalkIndustrial Catwalk
Who uses itFashion modelsWorkers, technicians

When you encounter the word catwalk, the context will almost always make the meaning clear. If it's about fashion, modelling, or clothing — it's the runway. If it's about a building, a ship, a factory, or a theatre — it's the elevated walkway for workers.
